candidates.attacker_control: HTTP request query/body parameter names and the URL path are attacker-controlled. With `struts.enable.DynamicMethodInvocation=true` (or `=true` plus `struts.mapper.action.prefix.enabled=true`), a parameter name such as `method:%23...` / `action:x!<payload>` (percent-encoded '=' and '#' survive servlet decoding, and PrefixTrie.get matches 'method:' as a prefix) places arbitrary characters into ActionMapping.method, which Dispatcher.serviceAction (Dispatcher.java:550-555) forwards to ActionProxyFactory.createActionProxy.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that cleanupActionName IS applied to the action name (line 374) and that accepted/excluded pattern checkers guard ParametersInterceptor and CookieInterceptor, so the ordinary parameter path is protected. Verified the sink at DefaultActionInvocation.java:423 is a genuine OGNL evaluation rather than reflection-only. Verified the `method:`/`!` branches only execute when DMI is enabled and that DMI defaults to false (default.properties:109), so default-configured apps are not exposed by this path. Verified escaping in DefaultActionProxy does not neutralize OGNL metacharacters but does escape quotes/slashes, which complicates (without necessarily preventing) context-manipulation payloads; SecurityMemberAccess and OgnlUtil excluded classes/packages further constrain the expression. No runtime execution or payload validation was performed.
candidates.impact: Expression-language (OGNL) injection in the framework core. Depending on the OGNL/member-access restrictions of the deployment, an unauthenticated remote user can read/mutate stack and context objects and, via known OGNL context-manipulation techniques, escalate to arbitrary method/static access and remote code execution under the web application's privileges. Failure modes are also a remote denial of service. The same missing sanitization leaves the URL namespace unsanitized (defense-in-depth gap).
candidates.prerequisites: The deployment must have Dynamic Method Invocation enabled (struts.enable.DynamicMethodInvocation=true; false by default since 2.3.15.3) — for the `action:` prefix variant, struts.mapper.action.prefix.enabled=true as well. The action mapping must resolve to an existing action so that prepare()/isAllowedMethod passes. Exploitation also depends on the OGNL context restrictions in OgnlValueStack/SecurityMemberAccess (excludedClasses/excludedPackageNamePatterns, allowStaticMethodAccess=false); the HTML/ECMAScript escaping in DefaultActionProxy removes quotes and slashes but leaves the OGNL metacharacters needed for expression injection and context manipulation.
candidates.root_cause: DefaultActionMapper applies cleanupActionName only to the action name, never to the method it extracts. In the `method:` prefix ParameterAction the raw parameter-name suffix is stored via mapping.setMethod(key.substring("method:".length())) (DefaultActionMapper.java:136-141); the `action:` prefix path stores the raw `!method` suffix (lines 144-155, setMethod at 152); and parseActionName stores the raw `!` suffix (lines 269-283, setMethod at 280). The namespace is likewise stored raw at line 373. Downstream, DefaultActionProxy only HTML/ECMAScript-escapes the method (DefaultActionProxy.java:83-87) — parentheses, brackets, '#', '.', '@', ',', '=' survive — and DefaultActionInvocation.invokeAction concatenates the attacker-controlled method name into an OGNL expression and evaluates it: `ognlUtil.getValue(methodName + "()", getStack().getContext(), action)` (DefaultActionInvocation.java:410-424). ActionConfig.isAllowedMethod adds no restriction in the common configuration because allowedMethods defaults to the '*' wildcard (ActionConfig.java:137-143), so any method string passes when DMI is enabled.
candidates.title: URL-supplied action method name reaches OGNL evaluation without expression sanitization (method:/! DMI vector)
candidates.trace: Request -> FilterDispatcher/Dispatcher.serviceAction -> DefaultActionMapper.getMapping -> handleSpecialParameters -> PrefixTrie 'method:' ParameterAction (raw method stored, no cleanup) OR parseActionName ('!method' raw) -> ActionMapping.method -> Dispatcher.serviceAction (line 552-555) -> ActionProxyFactory.createActionProxy -> DefaultActionProxy (escapeHtml4/escapeEcmaScript only) -> DefaultActionProxy.prepare -> ActionConfig.isAllowedMethod (permissive when allowedMethods='*') -> DefaultActionInvocation.invokeAction -> ognlUtil.getValue(methodName + "()", stackContext, action) -> OGNL evaluation of attacker-shaped expression.
candidates.unverified: No runtime confirmation was possible: exploitability depends on the deployment enabling DMI, on OGNL 3.0.6 parsing/whitespace behavior, and on whether the SecurityMemberAccess restrictions can be bypassed from the method-name injection point; the exact real-world CVE/advisory mapping for this snapshot (e.g., an S2-023/S2-024/S2-032-family fix) could not be confirmed from the source alone. The upstream fix might additionally/alternatively tighten ActionConfig.isAllowedMethod or the `action:`/namespace paths.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-917 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an Expression Language Statement (OGNL injection)

coverage_summary: Coverage is limited to the 3867 model-visible files reported by get_source_scope (binary-like files skipped; 1 file excluded by name/path; JSP/FTL template assets are not present in the visible tree, so view-layer XSS issues could not be reviewed). I reviewed the P1 relation-index scope first: the index is explicitly partial (47 parsed files, 25 parse errors, 855 omitted files, no data-flow/control-flow/semantic resolution), so I treated it only as navigation and verified all cited edges in source text. I inspected URL-to-action mapping (DefaultActionMapper, ActionMapping, Dispatcher.serviceAction, DefaultActionProxy, DefaultActionInvocation), the parameter/OGNL trust boundary (ParametersInterceptor, Accepted/ExcludedPatternsChecker, OgnlUtil, OgnlValueStack, SecurityMemberAccess, StrutsRequestWrapper), interceptors (Cookie, Token, TokenSessionStore, Debugging, FileUpload, Checkbox, Scope, I18n, ActionMappingParameters, ConversionError, Parameters), results (ServletRedirectResult, HttpHeaderResult, XSLTResult, StrutsResultSupport), static resource serving, and the REST/JSON plugin content handlers. Not exhaustively reviewed: all 28 plugins, apps/bundles/archetypes, and generated/static JS assets.
limitations: No code execution, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run; all conclusions are static and none are runtime-confirmed.
The P1 relation index is partial and syntactic only: 855 omitted files, 25 parse errors, no call/data-flow or reachability proof; index labels and edges were re-verified in source where cited.
JSP/FTL/Velocity view templates are absent from the model-visible tree, so view-layer XSS and template-injection areas could not be assessed.
The upstream fix associated with this snapshot (VUL4J-32) could not be identified from available source evidence alone; the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed mapping to a specific CVE/advisory.
Exploitability of the OGNL-method candidate depends on non-default configuration (DMI enabled) and on OGNL 3.0.6/SecurityMemberAccess behavior that was not dynamically validated.

rejected_leads.lead: REST plugin XML deserialization: ContentTypeInterceptor (plugins/rest/.../ContentTypeInterceptor.java:52-67) passes the request body to XStreamHandler.toObject (plugins/rest/.../handler/XStreamHandler.java:43-50), which calls `new XStream().fromXML(in, target)` with no type whitelist; the rest plugin declares xstream as a compile dependency (plugins/rest/pom.xml:42-45). This is a genuine RCE-class untrusted-deserialization pattern (later CVE-2017-9805), but it belongs to a much later fix generation than this 2.3.20.1-SNAPSHOT state, requires the REST plugin plus an XML-consuming action, and is not the issue I judged most likely tied to this snapshot.
rejected_leads.reason: Real residual risk but wrong timeframe and plugin-specific; kept as backup lead only.

rejected_leads.lead: Namespace is never sanitized: DefaultActionMapper.parseNameAndNamespace sets mapping.setNamespace(namespace) raw (line 373), unlike the action name. Later Struts added allowedNamespaceNames/cleanupNamespaceName.
rejected_leads.reason: No concrete sink found in this snapshot where the URL-derived namespace is OGNL-evaluated or used for class loading; would be defense-in-depth, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: DebuggingInterceptor exposes an OGNL console/command mode (`?debug=command&expression=...`, DebuggingInterceptor.java:189-210) and is registered in the defaultStack (struts-default.xml:342).
rejected_leads.reason: The interception is gated on devMode (lines 144-149) and devMode defaults to false (default.properties:140); no missing gate could be demonstrated from source, so it does not meet the evidence bar.

rejected_leads.lead: Token/CSRF area: TokenHelper uses SecureRandom and clears session tokens after validation (TokenHelper.java:55, 188-225), so no weak-randomness or replay bypass was demonstrable; TokenSessionStoreInterceptor only replays an invocation already stored in the same session.
rejected_leads.reason: Source already contains the expected hardening; no attacker-controlled bypass found.

rejected_leads.lead: plugins/json JSONPopulator/JSONInterceptor and plugins/rest Jackson/JsonLib handlers populate action objects from request bodies
rejected_leads.reason: Population is limited to public bean setters with type conversion; no OGNL/class-loader sink or bypass of SecurityMemberAccess verified in source.

summary: Reviewed the assigned Apache Struts 2.3.20.1-SNAPSHOT source tree (3867 model-visible files; Java/XML/properties), focusing on the request-to-OGNL trust boundary in core/xwork. The strongest source-verifiable weakness is in the URL action-mapping path: DefaultActionMapper sanitizes the action *name* (cleanupActionName/allowedActionNames) but stores the attacker-supplied action *method* (and namespace) verbatim, and that method string is concatenated into an OGNL expression and evaluated in DefaultActionInvocation.invokeAction ("ognlUtil.getValue(methodName + \"()\", …)"). When dynamic method invocation is enabled, a request parameter named `method:<OGNL>` (or `action:name!<OGNL>` with the mapper action-prefix also enabled) therefore reaches OGNL evaluation with only HTML/ECMAScript escaping applied, which does not remove `#`, `[`, `]`, `(`, `)`, `.`, `@`, `,`, `=`. Other leads (REST-plugin XStream deserialization, DebuggingInterceptor console, token/randomness code, JSON populator) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed; the REST XStreamHandler is a real residual risk but belongs to a later CVE generation.
